Agua Caliente means hot water, and Native people used and considered these springs sacred long before anyone else showed up. Quiz: in 1895, a Captain Boyes drilled down just 70 feet. What did he hit? [[pause 4]] 112-degree hot water! He built a resort hotel, which burned down in a wildfire in 1923. Its replacement became the Sonoma Mission Inn. And in World War Two, the Navy borrowed it as a rest centre for sailors and Marines back from the Pacific, including those Guadalcanal veterans. From one of the worst battles in history, straight to soft beds and cherry pie.

This one's a darker story, but an important one. Off to the west, near the village of Eldridge, are the grounds of the Sonoma Developmental Center, which for over a century was a big state institution for people with developmental disabilities. It opened here in 1891. California passed a forced sterilisation law in 1909, only the third state to do so. From 1918, the superintendent here, F. O. Butler, was a big believer in it, and personally performed at least a thousand operations. The centre even admitted people just to sterilise them and send them home. It was said to have sterilised more people than any other institution in the world, and risky medical experiments on residents went on into the 1960s. It finally closed at the end of 2018. Not every story on a road trip is a happy one, but this one's worth knowing.

Up on the slopes of Sonoma Mountain, above the village of Glen Ellen, is the ranch of Jack London, and his life was as wild as his books. Born in San Francisco in 1876, he was an oyster pirate in the bay as a teenager, sailed off to the Klondike gold rush at 21, and came back a committed socialist. Quiz: in 1903 he sold The Call of the Wild, one of the most famous books ever, to a magazine. How much do you think he got for it? [[pause 5]] 750 dollars! In 1905 he bought an abandoned winery here and called it Beauty Ranch. Then he started building his dream house, Wolf House: 26 rooms, nine fireplaces, built of massive stone to survive earthquakes, with fancy new stuff like electric lights, refrigeration and even a built-in vacuum cleaner. He and his wife Charmian spent over 80,000 dollars on it. And then, on the 22nd of August 1913, just before they were due to move in, it burned down. He was devastated, deep in debt, and he died at the ranch in 1916, aged just forty. His ashes are under a rock from the ruins of Wolf House. He also wrote a novel called The Valley of the Moon, a translation of the Native name for the Sonoma Valley. You can still walk to the stone ruins today.

Here's something you could find in the gravel around here: natural volcanic glass! The geology maps around Glen Ellen and Kenwood show a layer called the Glen Ellen Formation: river gravel made mostly of eroded volcanic rock, famous for its pebbles of obsidian. Up in the hills there's a lava called the Rhyolite of Adobe Canyon, glassy and grey-white with swirly folded bands, about 5.3 million years old. Nearby Anna-dell State Park's whole history is written in this rock: Native Americans used its obsidian, and then, quiz, in the early 1900s people quarried its volcanic rock for something you've definitely walked on. What? [[pause 5]] Cobblestones! And some biologists say Anna-dell has the best untouched oak woodland anywhere.

This next town tried on more names than a teenager tries on outfits. Kenwood sits on an old Mexican ranch called Los Gee-lee-kose, granted in 1837 to a Scottish sea captain who never even lived on it. In 1850 he sold it to another Scot, William Hood, a cabinet-maker who'd climbed the mountain above the valley, fallen in love with the view, and made his fortune building houses in Gold Rush San Francisco to afford it. The mountain's now called Hood Mountain. When the railroad arrived in 1887, the town tried Rohrerville, then Los Gee-lee-kose, then South Los Gee-lee-kose. Quiz: why do you think people wanted to change it again? [[pause 4]] Nobody could pronounce Gee-lee-kose! So around 1895 they voted for Kenwood. Either because settlers came from Kenwood in Illinois, or because English families knew Kenwood House in London. Maybe both! Up to the north-east is Sugarloaf Ridge State Park. When the state planned to close it in 2011 to save money, a group of volunteers called Team Sugarloaf took it over and reopened it. They even run an observatory up there.

Welcome to Santa Rosa, the biggest city in California's wine country! And it has a creek with a pretty grim name. Let me explain. Before Europeans arrived, the Santa Rosa plain belonged to a powerful Poe-moe group called the Bitakomtara. They controlled it tightly: outsiders needed permission to pass through, and if they didn't ask, the penalties were harsh. They gathered for ceremonies on Santa Rosa Creek, near today's Spring Lake. Colonisation brought violence, enslavement and smallpox, and devastated them, though their descendants still live in the region. The first European home here was built in the 1830s by María López de Carrillo, a widow from San Diego, whose daughter had married General Vuh-lay-oh. Quiz: before she arrived, settlers from Sonoma used to slaughter cattle where two creeks meet, and one creek got named after it. Matanza means what in Spanish? [[pause 4]] Slaughter! So that's Matanzas Creek. Lovely. In the 1850s her son helped lay out the downtown grid around a central square, and the city still follows it.

Near downtown Santa Rosa is the house and garden of Luther Burbank, one of the most famous plant breeders who ever lived. And Julia, Adam, there's a really good chance you've eaten his work. He was born in Massachusetts in 1849, the thirteenth of fifteen kids. As a young man he bred a new potato, sold the rights for 150 dollars, and used the money to move to Santa Rosa in 1875. Inspired by Charles Darwin, he crossed plants on an enormous scale and created more than 800 varieties: the Shasta daisy, the Santa Rosa plum, a white blackberry, a spineless cactus for cattle. Quiz: a natural variant of his potato became the most widely grown potato in the United States. And a big share of one very famous fast-food chain's french fries are made from it. Which chain? [[pause 5]] McDonald's! The Russet Burbank is the classic french fry potato. So next time you have McDonald's fries, say thanks to Luther. He's buried in his garden here, under a cedar tree.

Okay, Peanuts fans! Santa Rosa was home to Charles Schulz, the creator of Charlie Brown and Snoopy. He grew up in Minnesota, the son of a barber, loved ice hockey, and moved out here in 1958. He kept drawing Peanuts right up until he died in 2000. In 1969 he and his wife built an ice rink here, and everyone calls it Snoopy's Home Ice. Quiz: what do you think the café inside the rink is called? [[pause 5]] The Warm Puppy! Every summer it hosts Snoopy's Senior World Hockey Tournament for older players from around the world. Down the street is the Charles M. Schulz Museum, with a 22-foot mural made of 3,588 Peanuts comic strips that together make a picture of Lucy holding the football for Charlie Brown. And here's my favourite Santa Rosa coincidence. Schulz's very first published drawing, in 1937, was of his family dog Spike, who ate pins, tacks and razor blades. He sent it to Ripley's Believe It or Not, and they ran it! And Robert Ripley, who created Believe It or Not? Born right here in Santa Rosa.

Believe it or not, Robert Ripley was born right here in Santa Rosa, in 1890. He left high school after his dad died, started drawing sports cartoons for newspapers at sixteen, and moved to New York in 1913. In 1918 he drew his very first Believe It or Not cartoon, all about weird facts and feats, and readers loved it. They started mailing him their own oddities: funny-shaped vegetables, strangely marked pets, you name it. He took his facts seriously enough to hire a full-time researcher. And by 1929 the panel was running in 360 newspapers in 17 languages, followed by radio and TV shows. Quiz: Ripley also held a sports title. Which sport? [[pause 5]] Handball! He was New York State handball champion in 1926. Believe it or not. A perfect Santa Rosan for a day full of oddities.

Okay, a little earthquake talk. Somewhere under this part of Santa Rosa runs one of the most dangerous faults in the Bay Area. You've probably heard of the Hayward Fault, under Berkeley and Oakland. Well, this side of the bay has its partner: the Rodgers Creek Fault, running right through Santa Rosa. In 2016 scientists showed the two are actually connected under San Pablo Bay, making one fault about 120 miles long, from north of Heldz-burg all the way to San Jose. It's the kind of fault where the ground on the other side slides sideways, to your right. Quiz: on the evening of the 1st of October 1969, Santa Rosa got hit by not one, but how many earthquakes, about an hour and twenty minutes apart? [[pause 4]] Two! Magnitude 5.6 and 5.7. Chimneys fell, sidewalks buckled, pipes burst, and one person died. The damage was worse than expected, and modelling suggests the city sits where a basin full of sediment amplifies the shaking. Luckily it was evening, so few people were on the streets. Afterwards the city started earthquake-proofing its old brick buildings.

Over the hill from Calistoga, Highway 128 drops into Knights Valley, a small, quiet valley with the warmest climate in Sonoma County. In 1843 the Mexican governor rewarded a soldier from the Sonoma garrison, José de los Santos Berreyesa, with almost 18,000 acres, which included this valley and even the hot springs at Calistoga. Quiz: what do you think he used this beautiful valley for? [[pause 4]] His own private hunting preserve! And the adobe hunting lodge he built is still standing. The English name comes from Thomas Knight, a guy from Maine who'd been one of the Bear Flag rebels in Sonoma in 1846. He bought a big chunk of the ranch, and his name stuck.

Chalk Hill has a secret: there's no chalk. The hills to the south-west are the Chalk Hill wine area, named after one prominent hill. Quiz: so what's the white stuff in the soil really? [[pause 4]] Volcanic ash! White tuff, from the eruptions of the Mount Saint Huh-lee-nuh area, the same volcanism that turned the Petrified Forest to stone. It's said to be great for white grapes, and there's a warm band of air here, so harvest often comes in September, weeks before the neighbours. A bit further on, along Alexander Valley Road, the maps show a basalt lava flow and that obsidian-studded Glen Ellen gravel again. These are some of the last outposts of the big volcanic field, before the land turns to the old sea-floor rocks closer to the coast.

You're entering the Alexander Valley, the big, vine-filled valley of the Russian River north of Heldz-burg. It's the largest and most fully planted wine region in Sonoma County, with more than a hundred wineries. The story starts with a ranch called Sotoyome, almost 49,000 acres, named after a Wah-po group. It went to Henry Fitch, a San Diego sea captain who was General Vuh-lay-oh's brother-in-law. Fitch never lived here. He hired a manager, Cyrus Alexander, with a deal that after four years, Alexander would get a chunk of land and some cattle. Alexander settled down, and the valley took his name, even though the American land commission later rejected his claim to it. Ouch. Quiz: Alexander's replacement as ranch manager was the brother of a very famous Wild West frontiersman. Who? [[pause 5]] Kit Carson! His brother Mose Carson ran the ranch after 1845. And a wine note: Jordan winery here, with its French-style château from 1976, had a long-time winemaker who was trained by André Chelly-stcheff, the Bowl-you legend from Rutherford.

Heldz-burg is named after a squatter, and it gave the world lemon pepper. Seriously. It sits on the Russian River where three famous wine regions meet: the Alexander Valley, the Dry Creek Valley and the Russian River Valley. The Poe-moe built villages along the river here. The name comes from Harmon Heald, an Ohio businessman who squatted on the land from 1850, then bought a piece of it in 1857 when the owners auctioned off land to pay their taxes. The railroad arrived in 1872. And when Prohibition shut the wineries of Dry Creek Valley, which had been one of California's top Zinfandel regions, a lot of the land was switched to plums and prunes. Quiz: what famous seasoning was first developed commercially here in 1967? It's in the title. [[pause 3]] Lemon pepper! Thanks, Heldz-burg. If you cross the old steel bridge into town, that's the Heldz-burg Memorial Bridge from 1921, one of only thirteen bridges of its design in the whole country. People have been crossing the river at this exact spot since the 1850s, and the beach next to it is still a favourite swimming spot.

Here's a strong woman for you: Isabelle Simi. Simi Winery was started in San Francisco in 1876 by two Italian brothers who'd come for the Gold Rush, and they moved it here in 1881, paying 2,250 dollars in gold coins. From 1904, Giuseppe Simi's daughter Isabelle ran it, and she kept making wine right through Prohibition, storing it in the stone cellars. So when Prohibition ended in 1933, Simi was one of the only wineries with wine ready to sell. Clever. And in 1973 Simi hired Maryann Graf, the first woman to graduate from an American university with a degree in winemaking. Just north of town, Lytton has had a wild run: a luxury resort in 1872, then a boys' military school, a sanitarium, and for decades an orphanage. In 2017, the Lytton Band of Poe-moe Indians bought it back for around 30 million dollars, after years of trying to recover land they'd lost.

Quiz: the town of Windsor, coming up, got its name from a Pony Express rider. Why do you think he chose Windsor? [[pause 4]] He thought the countryside looked like the grounds of Windsor Castle, back in his home country of England! He was Hiram Lewis, the first postmaster, in 1855. Long before that, it was a Southern Poe-moe village called Tsoliikawai, which means blackbird field. Windsor had a rough start to the 1900s: a fire wiped out the town centre in 1905, then the 1906 earthquake damaged buildings that were still being repaired. In World War Two, the army built an air base on the south side of town, now the Charles M. Schulz airport. And in 1943 there was even a camp here for German prisoners of war.

Westside Road is one of the prettiest drives in wine country, winding along the river through some of the most celebrated Pinot Noir country in California. Cool, foggy, gorgeous. But check out the rocks too. The geology maps show this road crossing old sea-floor sandstone that got dragged down into the Earth in a subduction zone, squeezed at huge pressure, and turned blue with a mineral called glaucophane, then somehow made it back to the surface. It's called blueschist, and it's rare all over the world. Quiz: why do you think it's so rare? [[pause 5]] Because it can only form deep in a subduction zone, and then it has to find its way all the way back up to the surface. Further along you'll pass may-lahnj, that fruitcake rock, and old river gravels on flat benches cut into the bedrock. So on this lovely, winding road, you're driving over bits of an ancient ocean floor that went down into the Earth and came back up.

Welcome to Sebastopol, which has one of the best name stories on the map. Quiz: the town was originally called Pine Grove. Then in the late 1850s, a bar fight broke out. And somehow that led to the new name. How? [[pause 6]] A bystander said the long, drawn-out brawl was like the siege of Sevastopol, a Russian port in the Crimean War. And the name stuck! Remember Yount-vill? It was going to be called Sebastopol too, but this town got there first. The Coast Mee-wok and Poe-moe were here first, and the town sits on top of several of their village sites. Later there was a busy Chinatown downtown from the 1880s. Then came the apples. Sebastopol called itself the Grah-ven-steen Apple Capital of the World. The Grah-ven-steen is an old Danish apple, from the 1600s or earlier: tart, juicy, perfect for apple sauce and cider, but it doesn't keep, so you can only get it in season. There's still a Grah-ven-steen Apple Fair every August. These days the old apple warehouses have turned into The Barlow, full of tasting rooms and restaurants.

Luther Burbank, our potato guy, needed more space than his Santa Rosa garden, so in 1885 he bought a farm here in the Gold Ridge area. Quiz: at its peak, how many plant experiments do you think he had going on this farm at once? [[pause 5]] Over 60,000, by some estimates! Three acres of it survive, with more than 250 of his plants, looked after entirely by volunteers. And Sebastopol used to have electric trolleys! From 1903 to 1947, the Petaluma and Santa Rosa Railway ran around the county, partly to break the big railroad's monopoly. All that's left is one passenger car in a museum, and its old stone power house on Petaluma Avenue, which has, very fittingly, been turned into a series of brew pubs.

Here's a surprise for a town twenty miles from the ocean. The geology maps show that Highway 116 north of Sebastopol runs for more than ten kilometres across an old sea floor! It's called the Wilson Grove Formation: pale sandstone laid down in the sea between about eleven and three million years ago, and in places it's full of broken-up seashells. So all this gentle Gold Ridge country around Sebastopol used to be under the ocean, and got lifted up as the Coast Ranges rose. To the east, the Santa Rosa plain is made of gravel washed out of the hills. And as we head north toward the river, the road crosses into much older, harder rock from that geological junk drawer, the Franciscan Complex.

Grayton, just off the highway, is a little apple town that turned into a wine town. And quiz: it was once at the very edge of an empire. Which one? [[pause 5]] The Russian Empire! Grayton is about as far south and east as Russian colonisation in the Americas ever reached. The Russians at Fort Ross on the coast needed food, so in 1836 their farm expert, Yegor Chernykh, set up a farm between here and Occidental, with barracks, vegetables, wheat, and a big vineyard. So Russians helped plant some of the first vines around here! There's a sadder story in these hills too. In 1851, many California tribes signed treaties promising them land, but the U.S. never ratified them. In 1920 the government bought fifteen acres near here for the homeless Coast Mee-wok and Poe-moe people of the area. When seventy-five people tried to move in, they found only three acres were livable. And in 1958, the government ended the rancheria altogether.

Freestone, population about thirty-two, is the gateway to the Bo-hee-mee-un Highway. It's named after a sandstone quarry, and it was the first historic district Sonoma County ever named, in 1974. And it has my favourite crime story of the trip. In 1876, a farmer built the Hinds Hotel here when he heard the railroad was coming, and the carpenters building the railway line stayed there. Quiz: according to first-hand reports, the innkeeper came up with a sneaky plan to keep his guests around longer. What did he do? [[pause 6]] He had parts of the bridge they were building secretly burned at night, so the job would take longer! He went to jail for it. Customer retention, Wild West style. And in the 1970s, the old hotel was the party headquarters for the artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude while they built their famous Running Fence.

This next town has a creek named after a sailor who jumped ship, and a commune that tried to give its land to God. Welcome to Occidental! It was founded in 1876 as a stop on a railroad from the Saw-suh-lee-toe ferry up to the redwoods. A local landowner, a Danish sailor known as Dutch Bill Howard, who'd jumped ship in San Francisco Bay in 1849, gave the railroad its right-of-way. In return he got a free lifetime train pass, and the station was named after him. The creek next to the road is still Dutch Bill Creek. The railroad started a timber boom, and by 1877 there were six sawmills here. Then, a hundred years later: hippies! In 1966 Lou Gottlieb, from the folk band the Limeliters, bought land near here, and in 1967 he opened it to anyone who wanted to live there. Morning Star Ranch drew hundreds of people from San Francisco's Haight-Ashbury, and the county answered with arrests and bulldozers. Quiz: in 1969, Gottlieb tried to transfer the land to a new owner, to get the county off his back. Who? [[pause 5]] God! He deeded the land to God. The courts did not accept God as the owner.

Quiz: how much would you pay for a plot of land twenty-five feet by twelve, with a one-room cabin on it? [[pause 4]] In 1898, right here, it cost seventy-five dollars. This is Camp Meeker, named after Melvin Cyrus Meeker, a lumber baron who opened mills here around 1866. These redwoods built San Francisco, and then, after 1906, rebuilt it. Meeker is the same guy who sold the Bo-hee-mee-un Grove land to the Bo-hee-mee-un Club. Once the trees were cut down, he chopped the land into those tiny lots and sold them to San Franciscans wanting a summer escape. Now it's a little village of about 425 people tucked among the new redwoods, with some roads so steep and narrow they feel like old railway tracks. And the creek has become a happy conservation story: wild coho salmon came back to spawn in 2001, young salmon have been released here since 2006, and in 2009 an old swimming-hole dam, one of the worst salmon blockers in the whole watershed, was swapped for a footbridge.

The land from the Golden Gate up to the Sonoma coast, and east to Sonoma Creek, was home to the Coast Mee-wok. That includes the hills around Sebastopol and Freestone and the lower Sonoma Valley. They lived in small bands with no central government. In spring they headed to the coast for salmon, shellfish and seaweed. The rest of the year, acorns were the staple, plus deer and rabbit. Quiz: Coast Mee-wok hunters had a clever trick for sneaking up on deer. What do you think they did? [[pause 5]] They rubbed themselves with a plant called Brewer's angelica to hide their scent! They also drank yerba buena tea as medicine, made tattoo ink from burned poison oak, and built cone-shaped houses called kotcha from tule reeds or redwood bark. Amazing basket makers too. The word Mee-wok just means people. Within a couple of generations of the Spanish arriving, the people of this region lost their land and were devastated by disease. Later, broken federal treaties left them landless. If you ever visit Point Reyes, there's a recreated Coast Mee-wok village there called Koo-lay Lock-low.

You're on the Silverado Trail, the quieter road up the east side of the Napa Valley, 29 miles long. And quiz: back in the 1880s, travellers on this road had to watch out for a famous someone. Who? [[pause 4]] A stagecoach robber called Black Bart! He preyed on travellers here. Things got safer when a motor bus service started in 1910. The road started in 1852 as a trail used when floods made the main valley road impassable. Later it became the wagon road for the mercury mines on Mount Saint Huh-lee-nuh, and the first permanent road between Napa and Calistoga. Silver was found in the valley in 1858. Today there are at least forty wineries along it, and every March it hosts the Napa Valley Marathon. The hills just east of Napa are called Coombsville, after Nathan Coombs, the guy who founded Napa. Volcanic soil, and fog that rolls in early and hangs around late.

Okay, wine fans, sit up! You're about to pass the vineyard that beat the French. This is the Stags Leap District, a tiny pocket of land only about one mile by three, with hills on three sides. Here's the story. Warren Win-ee-ar-ski fell in love with wine while spending a year in Italy studying Machiavelli. He moved his family to Napa in 1968 and worked at Robert Mon-dah-vee's new winery. Then he tasted a homemade wine from a neighbour, Nathan Fay, and thought, this is it. In 1970 he bought the 44 acres next door. Quiz: what was growing on the land when he bought it? [[pause 5]] Prunes, cherries and walnuts! He ripped them out and planted Cabernet. And his 1973 Cabernet went to Paris in 1976 and took first place, beating Château Mouton-Rothschild and Haut-Brion. The magazine Decanter called it a victory that put California on the winemaking map. And the soil here is special: clay from the Napa River mixed with volcanic stuff washed down from the Vacka Mountains.

Two wineries along here tell two sides of the Napa story. First, Frog's Leap, started in 1981 by a doctor and a winemaker at a spot known as Frog Farm. Quiz: the winemaker got his start at a very famous winery nearby. Can you guess which, from the name? [[pause 4]] Stag's Leap! Frog Farm plus Stag's Leap equals Frog's Leap. And the corks say Ribbit. But behind the jokes, it's serious stuff: it was the first Napa winery to use certified organic grapes, the vines aren't irrigated, and since 2005 solar panels supply most of its power. Then Heitz Cellar, from 1961, back when Napa had only about two dozen wineries left. Joe Heitz, a farm boy from Illinois, was one of the first seven people ever to graduate from UC Davis in winemaking, in 1951. He trained under the legendary Chelly-stcheff, bought a little vineyard for 5,000 dollars, and his Martha's Vineyard Cabernet became a Napa legend. It was even one of the reds tasted in Paris in 1976.

Look east around Saint Huh-lee-nuh. That forested ridge is Howell Mountain. And here's a surprise: Napa was winning medals in Paris long before 1976! Two French winemakers set up there in 1877, and Charles Krug planted about a hundred acres by 1884. Then a man called W. S. Keyes planted his vineyard in 1880. Quiz: at the Paris Exposition of 1899, what did his wines win? [[pause 4]] Gold and bronze medals! And in 1904, his claret won the grand prize at the St. Louis World's Fair. So 1976 wasn't the first time Napa impressed the French. It was just the most famous.

Mark Twain and Clark Gable both came to soak in springs near here. Near Saint Huh-lee-nuh was White Sulphur Springs, said to be the oldest warm-spring resort in Northern California, opened in 1852. Native people used the springs long before that. In the late 1800s, rich San Franciscans got here by steamboat, then train, then stagecoach. Quiz: at its peak, how many guests could the grand hotel hold? [[pause 4]] A thousand! After the 1906 earthquake it housed refugees. Sadly, fire was always its enemy: three grand hotels burned over the years, and the 2020 Glass Fire destroyed most of what was left.

You're climbing Spring Mountain Road into the My-uh-kah-muss. Quiz: where's the actual Spring Mountain? [[pause 4]] Trick question! There isn't one. Spring Mountain was the name for a whole green, well-watered area of hills full of springs and little streams, not one peak. It was one of the first places in Napa recognised for grapes. The first documented vineyard was Charles Lemme's La Perla, planted in 1874, and in the 1880s the Beringer brothers planted up here too. The vineyards are on steep slopes, so the crops are small: it makes less than two percent of Napa's wine. Up over the county line, the road becomes Saint Huh-lee-nuh Road and drops down toward the start of Mark West Creek.

You're crossing a mountain range that the federal government couldn't decide how to spell! These are the My-uh-kah-muss Mountains, 52 miles long, separating the Napa and Sonoma valleys. The highest point is Cobb Mountain, 4,724 feet, and the rain that falls up here ends up in Pew-tah Creek, Sonoma Creek, Santa Rosa Creek and Mark West Creek. The name probably comes from a Wah-po village called Maiya'kma, near Calistoga. Quiz: the federal naming board made one decision on the spelling, then reversed it in 1941. Which spelling did they finally pick? [[pause 5]] Mayacmas! Without the second a. And plenty of people still write My-uh-kah-muss. And there's still a creek called Mah-kah-muh. So, honestly, spell it however you like. The road you're on crosses a volcanic landscape: white pumice from an eruption about 4.84 million years ago, grey lava from about 7.9 million, and swirly glassy lava from about 5.3 million. And about ten million years ago, these mountains were probably covered in cypress forest.

Two wineries went to war with the federal government over one word: Calistoga! Here's the deal. Official wine regions are created by the federal government, and once one exists, wineries have to use mostly grapes from that area to put its name on the label. In 2003, Bo Barrett of Chateau Monteh-lay-nuh asked for a Calistoga wine region. But two wineries, Calistoga Cellars and Calistoga Estate, already had Calistoga in their brand names. Quiz: what do you think they'd have to do if the region was approved? [[pause 5]] Either use at least 85 percent Calistoga grapes, or change their names! They fought it hard. It finally got approved in 2009, and they got three years to comply. Next door, Diamond Mountain had a fight over one word too, and the owners of a winery with that trademark won, so it's officially the Diamond Mountain District. And in Sonoma, a giant region called Northern Sonoma was created in 1985 largely because of the huge Gallo winery.

Okay, let's talk about the event that made Sacramento, and, honestly, most of what you'll see today. On the 24th of January 1848, James Marshall was building a sawmill for the pioneer John Sutter, up the American River, when he spotted something shiny in the water. Gold! Sutter tried to keep it secret, because he was worried a rush would wreck his plans for a farming empire. Quiz: who do you think spread the news anyway? Hint: you've already met him today. [[pause 5]] Sam Brannan! And about 300,000 people poured into California. San Francisco went from about 200 people in 1846 to around 36,000 by 1852, and California became a state in 1850. The Gold Rush echoes through this whole trip. West Sacramento was a rest stop for miners. Dixon started as a halfway stop for them. Alfred Tubbs made his fortune selling rope to the rush, then founded Chateau Monteh-lay-nuh. Dr. Bale of the grist mill went off mining and died of a fever. And all those new people were thirsty, so vineyards spread across Napa and Sonoma in the 1850s. But it was a catastrophe for Native Californians. Disease, hunger and violence made their populations collapse, and whole tribes were driven from their land, including the Pat-win of this valley.

South of the freeway, out of sight, is one of the most important places in California: the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta. The Yo-lo Bypass floods drain into it, and so does about half of all the water that runs off California's land. Here's how it formed. Around 560,000 years ago, water broke through the coastal mountains and carved the Car-keen-ess Strait and San Francisco Bay. All the rivers had to squeeze out through that one narrow gap, which slowed them down. The tides pushed back up and slowed them even more, so the rivers dropped their mud and built a huge freshwater marsh full of channels and peat islands. Then people drained it. Today there are about 57 reclaimed islands, ringed by 1,100 miles of levees. Quiz: when you drain peat soil, something weird happens to the land. What? [[pause 5]] It sinks! The peat breaks down and blows away, so a lot of the Delta now sits below sea level, behind its levees. That's why it's nicknamed California's Holland. And giant pumps at the south end send Delta water to farms and to the cities of Southern California. So pretty much every California water fight ends up here.

Here's a handy one if you ever drive this valley in winter. From November to March, after the first big rains, the Central Valley gets something called tule fog, named after the tule reeds that used to cover the wetlands. On long, still winter nights, the damp ground cools fast, and the cold air near the ground gets trapped under warmer air above, until it turns into a thick, low blanket of fog. It can stretch over 400 miles, from Bakersfield to Red Bluff. Quiz: in 2005, tule fog was the number one cause of what in California? [[pause 4]] Weather-related car accidents! So if you ever see this valley disappear into a white wall on a winter morning, slow way down. Today, in late October, we're just ahead of the season. Phew.

Every vineyard and orchard you pass depends on people who rarely show up in the wine brochures. Here's their story. The first workers were Native Californians, often forced. The Pat-win were made to work for free on ranches and in mines, and by 1870 only a few Native people remained in the Napa Valley, working as labourers and servants. In the late 1800s, Chinese and Japanese immigrants worked Vacka-vill's orchards. In World War Two there was even a camp of German prisoners of war near Windsor, put to work. The biggest change was the Bracero Program, a deal between the U.S. and Mexico that started in Stockton in August 1942 to fill wartime labour shortages. Over 22 years, it offered millions of contracts to Mexican workers. Quiz: what minimum hourly wage were they promised? [[pause 4]] Thirty cents an hour. The programme ended in 1964, and economists later found that ending it pushed farms toward machines. Today, around a third of Napa County's people are Hispanic or Latino. And the tension between luxury and labour is very much alive: in 2026, Thomas Keller of the French Laundry opposed a plan for 120 apartments in Yount-vill for workers who'd been priced out of town.

Have you noticed something about the Napa Valley floor? There are basically no housing developments or shopping malls between the towns. That's not luck. It's one of the most important land decisions in California history. Neighbouring counties let big stretches of farmland turn into houses and shops. But in 1968, Napa's winemakers and civic leaders went the other way. Using a new state law that gave tax breaks for keeping land in farming, they created an agricultural preserve on the valley floor. Quiz: was Napa the first county in California to do this? [[pause 4]] Yes! It was the first one in the state. It started at 23,000 acres and grew to over 30,000. Then in 1990, voters went further and froze county zoning changes for thirty years, unless two-thirds of voters agreed. The fights never stop. Locals battled the Wine Train in the eighties. County rules even stop Castello dee Amo-roza from hosting weddings. And now the big fight is about whether the people who work here can afford to live here. The preserve kept the valley green. Who gets to live in it is the next argument.

Wine isn't the only crop around here with a complicated legal history. California has been at the front of cannabis politics for half a century. In 1972, it held the first ballot vote in the nation to legalise cannabis. Quiz: did it pass? [[pause 4]] Nope! It failed. But in 1996, California became the first state to legalise medical cannabis, and in 2016, voters legalised recreational use, with 57 percent of the vote. Legalisation turned out to be messy. Growers had to register and get permits, and more than half of the medical dispensaries closed. Legal businesses pay hefty taxes, while illegal growers keep going in remote rural areas. And it's all still illegal under federal law. So, a bit like the winemakers during Prohibition, today's cannabis farmers live in a weird legal twilight zone between what the state allows and what Washington forbids.

We've met Russians again and again today: a river, a mountain, a farm near Grayton. So here's the whole story. Russian traders pushed east across Siberia and the North Pacific, and in 1799 they set up a colony in Alaska. Their business was fur, especially sea otters. From 1803, American ship captains took Alaska Native hunters down the California coast to hunt otters, and between 1805 and 1812 alone they gathered over 22,000 pelts. In 1812 the Russians built their own base, Fort Ross, on the Sonoma coast, in the land of the Kuh-shy-uh Poe-moe. It was super diverse: Native Californians, Native Alaskans, Russians, Finns and Swedes, all together. They explored the river and planted a farm and vineyard near Grayton. And the Spanish and Mexicans got so nervous that they built the mission at Sonoma partly to block them. Quiz: in 1841 the Russians decided to sell Fort Ross. They offered it to General Vuh-lay-oh, but the Mexican officials dithered. Who ended up buying it? [[pause 5]] John Sutter! The same Sutter on whose land gold was discovered seven years later. Small world.

Here's a wine story you won't hear in many tasting rooms. California's first wine grape was the Mission grape, brought by the Spanish, and it ruled until about 1880. Then the Gold Rush created thirsty customers, and Ah-go-stone Hair-uss-tee brought in cuttings from 165 of Europe's best vineyards. Charles Krug, a Prussian political dissident, learned winemaking from Hair-uss-tee before starting his own winery in Saint Huh-lee-nuh. And north of Santa Rosa, at the utopian colony of Fountain Grove, the vineyards were run by Nagasawa Kanaye. Quiz: what nickname do you think he earned? [[pause 4]] The Grape King of California! He was one of the biggest winemakers in the state, and he threw lavish dinners for guests like John Muir, Thomas Edison and Henry Ford. And according to the history books, Fountain Grove's cellars kept flowing right through Prohibition. Wink. It's a reminder that wine country's history is a lot more diverse than the fancy châteaux suggest: Spanish missionaries, a Hungarian adventurer, German and Italian immigrants, a Finnish sea captain, and a Grape King, all on land that was Poe-moe, Wah-po, Mee-wok and Pat-win for thousands of years.

Good morning, road-trippers! Julia, Adam, our heroic driver: welcome to day two. And what a day. We're following the Russian River all the way to the ocean. Then it's down the wild Sonoma Coast to Bo-day-guh Bay, where Alfred Hitchcock made birds terrifying. After that, either along Toe-mah-less Bay and the Point Reyes coast, or inland through Petaluma, to the giant redwoods of Muir Woods. Then over the Golden Gate Bridge and through San Francisco to the airport. Quick warm-up quiz while you finish your coffee. Today we're going to cross the biggest, most famous fault line in America, more than once. What's it called? [[pause 4]] The San Andreas Fault! And here's the wild bit: by this afternoon we'll have driven on a different tectonic plate. Some of the land we're passing is moving north at about an inch a year. More on that later. Let's go find the ocean!

Picture this road with a little narrow-gauge train chugging along beside the river. From the 1870s, the North Pacific Coast Railroad ran from Cah-zuh-dair-oh, through Mon-tee Ree-oh and Duncans Mills, all the way down to the Saw-suh-lee-toe ferry. And you'll hear its name again and again today, because it also stopped at Valley Ford, Toe-mah-less, Marshall and Point Reyes Station. At first it hauled redwood lumber to build San Francisco. In 1877 Alexander Duncan set up a sawmill right here, and the town grew up around it, with two hotels, a saloon, a blacksmith and a livery stable. When the mills moved on, the trains started carrying San Franciscans up to summer cabins instead. Mon-tee Ree-oh, back there, branded itself Vacation Wonderland, and even had a seven-story hotel downtown. Parts of the 1942 Oscar-winning film Holiday Inn were shot at a resort in Mon-tee Ree-oh. Quiz: the railroad shut down in the 1930s, and Duncans Mills slowly faded. Then, in 1976, something brought it back to life. What do you think? [[pause 5]] America's two-hundredth birthday! A Bicentennial restoration project fixed up the old buildings. And there's still an original depot here, with some of the old railroad cars.

There it is! The Russian River meets the Pacific Ocean, right here at Jenner. Population: about a hundred and twenty. Quick reminder of why it's called the Russian River. Russians from the Russian-American Company explored it in the early 1800s, when they set up Fort Ross, about ten miles up the coast. They called it the Slah-vyahn-kuh. The Poe-moe had much older names for it, including Bee-dahp-tay, big river. The town is named after Dr. Elijah Jenner, a dentist and inventor from Vermont who came west for the Gold Rush in 1850. While he was mining, he designed a pump that could lift water a hundred feet. Quiz: when he applied for the patent, he sent a model of the pump. What was so special about it? [[pause 5]] It was made of pure gold! It's the only golden model the Patent Office has ever received. A true Gold Rush flex. By 1854 the family had settled here at the mouth of the river. And watch the river mouth. In summer, the waves build a sandbar right across it, and the river turns into a lagoon until the water gets high enough to break through. In late fall and winter, when the sandbar's breached, the sheltered beach on the north side is a favourite spot for harbor seals to have their pups.

Okay, movie quiz! Down on the left is Goat Rock Beach, with that huge flat-topped rock barely hanging on to the land. In 1985, a very famous adventure movie, about a group of kids hunting for pirate treasure, filmed its ending on this beach. Which movie? [[pause 5]] The Goonies! Goonies never say die. Now look at all those rocks sticking out of the sea. They're called sea stacks, and here's how they got there. For about 170 million years, an ocean plate was diving under North America. It scraped off pillow lava, chert and sandstone, and crushed it all into may-lahnj, which is a jumble of hard blocks floating in a softer, ground-up rock. When the waves hit it, the soft stuff washes away and the hard blocks are left standing in the sea. Goat Rock is one big hard block of grey-wacky sandstone. And here's a cool one. About a mile south of the river there's a rock of blueschist with rubbing marks two to four meters up. That's too high for cows. Scientists think mammoths made them, using it as a back-scratcher! Mammoths are believed to have roamed here as recently as 40,000 years ago. Careful if you stop, though: the beach drops off steeply and there's a nasty rip current.

This is the Sonoma Coast, seventeen miles of state beaches running all the way down to Bo-day-guh Head. Little coves, big rocks, cliffs, and fog that can roll in fast. Quiz: those bluffs are made of soft soil, and the ocean's chewing away at them. How much land do you think this coast loses in an average year? [[pause 5]] One to three feet a year! More in a stormy winter. It's also rising. Over the ages this land has been pushed up, which is why you're driving on a flat shelf above the beach. It's called a marine terrace: old sea floor, lifted up. Some of those sea stacks are even standing up on the terrace, away from the water, because they started life on the sea floor before it rose. Look out to sea for gray whales, harbor seals and California sea lions. The Coast Mee-wok and Poe-moe lived along here for a very long time, and dozens of their old shell middens, basically ancient kitchen garbage heaps, have been found on this coast. The Russians cut down the old-growth forest above the coastal prairie in the early 1800s, and later it became part of a Mexican ranch called Rancho Bo-day-guh.

Welcome to Bo-day-guh Bay! Fishing boats, salty air, and a harbor tucked behind that long headland. The bay is named after Juan Francisco de la Bo-day-guh y Kwah-druh, a Spanish naval officer who sailed in here in 1775. In 1793 the Spanish sent a little garrison with four cannons, because they'd heard the English might show up. They didn't, so the guns went back to Monterey. And then guess who did show up? The Russians! In 1809, before they built Fort Ross, they put up the first Russian buildings in California here, and called it Port Room-yahnt-sev, after their foreign minister. Hollywood loves this town. Hitchcock filmed The Birds here, which I'll tell you about in a second. But there's also The Fog, I Know What You Did Last Summer, and The Russians Are Coming, the Russians Are Coming. Quiz: in 2021, a famous TV comedy needed to film a season in Ireland, but COVID made that impossible. So Bo-day-guh Bay played Ireland instead! Which show? [[pause 5]] It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia! A Northern California fishing village pretending to be Ireland. Honestly, with the fog, it works.

Okay, The Birds! In 1963, Alfred Hitchcock made a horror film about birds suddenly, inexplicably attacking the people of Bo-day-guh Bay. Tippy Hed-ren, in her first film, plays a San Francisco socialite who drives up here with a pair of lovebirds, and things go very badly. Gulls at the dock, crows at the schoolhouse, sparrows pouring down the chimney. Quiz: Hitchcock was partly inspired by a real event in 1961, when thousands of seabirds dive-bombed a California seaside town called Cap-ih-toe-luh, crashing into cars and dropping half-eaten fish on people's lawns. Gross. What do you think really caused it? [[pause 5]] Toxic algae! It poisoned the birds. But nobody knew that in the 1960s. And most of the birds in the movie are real. The gulls were caught at the San Francisco garbage dump. Some of the crows were actually ravens. There were 370 special-effects shots, and the final shot was built out of 32 separate pieces. The film was shot around two places, Bo-day-guh Bay and the inland village of Bo-day-guh, edited to look like one town. The church and the schoolhouse are just up the road in Bo-day-guh. A darker footnote: decades later, Tippy Hed-ren said Hitchcock harassed her during the filming. Today the film's considered one of the greatest horror movies ever made.

Across the harbor is Bo-day-guh Head, and it has a hole in it. Literally. Here's the story. In the late 1950s and early 60s, the utility company PG&E planned to build a nuclear power plant on Bo-day-guh Head. It was meant to be the first commercially viable nuclear plant in the United States. The fishermen were worried about their livelihoods. And a local woman, Rose Gaffney, who owned land on the headland, refused to sell, sued the company, and invited government officials to come and see the fault lines on the site for themselves. Quiz: in June 1963, the protesters released 1,500 of something into the air with a warning message attached. What? [[pause 4]] Helium balloons! The message said each one could represent a radioactive molecule of strontium 90 or iodine 131. In 1964, after a negative review by the Atomic Energy Commission, PG&E gave up. Historians call it the birth of the anti-nuclear movement. And the real clincher: the San Andreas Fault runs right between Bo-day-guh Head and the mainland. Bo-day-guh Head is on the Pacific Plate, the town's on the North American Plate. In the 1906 earthquake, the headland jumped about fifteen feet. Its rock is granite, related to the Sierra Nevada, carried north hundreds of miles along the fault. By then they'd already dug the pit for the reactor. It filled with water, and locals call it the Hole in the Head.

This little village is Bo-day-guh, once called Bo-day-guh Corners, to tell it apart from the port down by the water. There used to be two Coast Mee-wok villages in the area. Then the Russians settled in the Salmon Creek valley here in 1809. Quiz: around 1843, John Sutter bought land from the departing Russians, including this area. What did the deal include? Guess one thing. [[pause 5]] Some hunting rights, a small boat, several rusty cannons and some old muskets! What a bargain. In 1843 a Captain Stephen Smith also built the first lumber mill on the West Coast near here. Then the town proper began in 1853 with a saloon, a blacksmith and a hotel. Naturally. In 1859, shipbuilders built the Saint Teresa of Avila Church. And if both church and schoolhouse look familiar, that's because the church and schoolhouse in The Birds are right here on the Bo-day-guh Highway. That's the school where the crows gather on the jungle gym. Geology note: the geology maps show the rock around here is the Wilson Grove Formation, from the late Miocene and Pliocene, very roughly ten to three million years ago. It's the same sea-floor sandstone we met back in Sebastopol.

Tiny Valley Ford, population about a hundred and fifty. Dairy country: rolling green hills and cows. The Coast Mee-wok had a village here called Eh-wah-palt. In the 1850s there was a grain mill, and from 1876 the North Pacific Coast Railroad stopped here, so ranchers and fishers could ship their produce down to San Francisco. Quiz: in 1976, a famous pair of artists, Christo and Jeanne-Claude, built a giant artwork that passed right through Valley Ford, running from Co-tah-tee all the way to Bo-day-guh Bay. What do you think it was? [[pause 5]] A fence! Running Fence: a long white fabric fence across the hills, all the way to the ocean. Two more fun facts. If anyone in the car plays guitar: Shubb, the company that makes capos, has its headquarters right here. And a less fun fact: the dairies have put so much nitrate into the groundwater that in 2017 the state warned pregnant women and babies not to drink the town's well water, and some restaurants truck their water in from Petaluma.

Welcome to Marin County! And to Toe-mah-less, population just under two hundred, perched above Keys Creek. The Coast Mee-wok had many villages around here, including one called Oo-too-mee-uh, near the town. The post office opened in 1854, spelled Tomalles with two L's, and later it lost one. The North Pacific Coast Railroad came through in the 1870s. Quiz: Toe-mah-less sits close to the San Andreas Fault. How can you still see the damage from the 1906 earthquake here? [[pause 5]] In the cemetery! One of the town's two cemeteries is older than the earthquake, and the old graves are still damaged. It shows how far the shaking reached. Speaking of Marin: Vuh-lay-oh, the general from yesterday in Sonoma, said the county was named after Marin, a Coast Mee-wok leader. More on him later.

That long, skinny bay is Toe-mah-less Bay: about fifteen miles long, only a mile wide, and shallow, about eighteen feet deep on average. Quiz: in 1603, Spanish explorers from the Viz-kuh-ee-no expedition found this bay. What did they think it was? [[pause 4]] A river! They called it the Rio Grande de San Sebastián. Easy mistake, look at it. But it's not a river, it's a fault! Toe-mah-less Bay sits on a drowned stretch of the San Andreas Fault. Everything on the far side, the Point Reyes Peninsula, is on the Pacific Plate. You're on the North American Plate. The fault cuts through the peninsula, from Toe-mah-less Bay in the north to Buh-lee-nus Lagoon in the south, and we'll follow it nearly the whole way. The Coast Mee-wok had villages all around the bay. Shells and clams from the bay's shore weren't just food: they were used as money. And just across the peninsula, the English captain Francis Drake is thought to have landed in 1579. That story's coming up.

This stretch of shoreline is Marshall, and if anyone's hungry, you're in luck: oysters! The town is named after the Marshalls, four brothers who started dairy farming here in the 1850s. The railroad stopped here from the 1870s too. There's still some dairy, with the Straus Family Creamery based here. But these days the big business is oysters and clams. Quiz: oyster farming is a major industry on Toe-mah-less Bay. Can you name either of the two biggest producers? I'll give you a hint: one of them is named after an animal. [[pause 5]] Hog Island Oyster Company, and Toe-mah-less Bay Oyster Company! Both sell to the public, and both have picnic grounds on this east shore. If you stop, the classic move is a bag of oysters at a picnic table by the water. The cows on the hills across the bay graze on ranches leased from Point Reyes National Seashore, and that's a whole controversy for another day.

Welcome to Point Reyes Station, the little hub town for the Point Reyes peninsula. It started as the railroad's terminus stop. When the trains arrived in 1875 it was called Oh-lee-muh Station. Quiz: in 1891 alone, how many times did the town's name change? [[pause 4]] Three times! First to Marin, then back to Point Reyes, then finally to Point Reyes Station. Make up your mind! Fun fact: it used to be a real port on Toe-mah-less Bay. But cattle and European grasses caused erosion, and silt, little dams and landfill for farming raised up the old salt marshes. Now the town is nearly a mile from the nearest tidal flats. And it sits just east of the San Andreas Fault. Over at the Bear Valley Visitor Center, near Oh-lee-muh, there's the Earthquake Trail, where you can see a rift left by the 1906 earthquake.

This crossroads is Oh-lee-muh. Quiz: the name comes from a Coast Mee-wok place name. It's an animal, plus valley. Which animal? [[pause 4]] Coyote! Oh-lee-muh means coyote valley. For years people believed Oh-lee-muh was the epicenter of the great 1906 earthquake, because the ground nearby moved so much. The rifts are still visible on a hiking path. Modern research points to an epicenter offshore, near Daly City, which we'll drive through this afternoon. A bit of music history: Oh-lee-muh got its own song in the late 1960s, Hippie from Oh-lee-muh, by The Youngbloods, a cheeky reply to Merle Haggard's Okie from Muskogee. And just up Bear Valley Road, a quarter mile from town, is the visitor center for Point Reyes National Seashore, with Koo-lay Lock-low, a reconstructed Coast Mee-wok village. The Coast Mee-wok's descendants formed the Federated Indians of Grayton Rancheria, which won federal recognition in 2000, and they hold ceremonies at Koo-lay Lock-low.

Okay, story time. On the 17th of June, 1579, the English sea captain Francis Drake sailed into a sheltered cove just over those hills. His ship, the Golden Hind, needed repairs. He'd spent months raiding Spanish towns and treasure ships along the Pacific coast, and he was about to sail home the long way, right round the world. He stayed about five weeks, and got on well with the Coast Mee-wok who lived here. He named the land New Albion, partly because the white cliffs reminded him of England, and claimed it for Queen Elizabeth the First. He nailed up a brass plate with a sixpence showing the Queen's face. Then on the 23rd of July he sailed away, without leaving a colony, and got back to England in September 1580. People argued about exactly where he landed for centuries. Quiz: one of the best clues came from archaeologists. Nearly a hundred pieces of something were found near the cove, which had to have come from Drake. What do you think? [[pause 6]] Chinese porcelain! Broken dishes that Drake had taken from a Spanish treasure ship and dumped here while lightening his ship for repairs. In 2021 California officially named Drake's Cove, inside Point Reyes National Seashore, as the site of New Albion. And the name Point Reyes? On the 6th of January 1603, Sebastián Viz-kuh-ee-no sighted the headland on Three Kings' Day, so he called it la Punta de los Reyes, the Point of the Kings.

Out there on the Point Reyes peninsula is one of the wildest corners of California. A congressman named Clem Miller wrote the bill in 1962 to protect it, because developers wanted to build on the slopes above Drakes Bay. Now about half of it is wilderness. Quiz: when Europeans arrived, there were maybe half a million tule elk in California. By the 1870s, people thought they were extinct. How many do you think were found, hiding in a marsh in the Central Valley? [[pause 5]] One breeding pair! Just two! Genetic studies fit the idea that today's tule elk all descend from that tiny group. In 1978, ten were brought to Toe-mah-less Point here, and after a rough start, from 1981 they were breeding at full speed. Then the elephant seals came back too. They started a breeding colony in 1981. And here's my favourite: in January 2019, during a government shutdown, with no rangers working, the elephant seals moved onto Drakes Beach and had their pups. In the parking lot! And at the very end of the point is the Point Reyes Lighthouse, first lit in 1870. Official records call it the windiest and foggiest spot on the Pacific Coast, with gales up to a hundred miles an hour. Quiz: most lighthouses are built up high so ships can see them from far away. This one is built low, down a cliff, at the bottom of about three hundred steps. Why? [[pause 5]] To get the light below the fog! Up top it would just disappear into the clouds.

Right now we're driving almost exactly along the San Andreas Fault. This straight valley, with Oh-lee-muh Creek, is the fault zone. To the north it sinks under Toe-mah-less Bay; to the south it runs under Buh-lee-nus Lagoon. Then it heads out to sea and comes back on land near Daly City. The fault runs about 750 miles through California. It's where two plates slide past each other. Quiz: the Pacific Plate, on your right, is moving north compared to the North American Plate. Roughly how fast? [[pause 5]] About an inch a year. But it doesn't slide smoothly. It sticks, builds up strain for decades, and then lets go all at once. In 1906, the ground along the fault shifted by up to twenty feet. After the 1906 earthquake, a Berkeley professor, Andrew Lawson, mapped all the fences and roads that had been sliced in half and shifted. They made an almost perfect line, right along a fault he'd found in 1895. He named it after the San Andreas Valley, down the peninsula. And that rock on the far side, the granite of Point Reyes and Bo-day-guh Head, is related to the Sierra Nevada. It's been carried hundreds of miles north along this fault.

Somewhere off to the right, across the lagoon, is Buh-lee-nus. You probably won't see a sign for it. Quiz: why not? [[pause 4]] Because the locals keep tearing them down! Every sign on Highway 1 pointing the way to Buh-lee-nus has been removed by residents. The county even put it to a vote, and the voters said, no more signs, thank you. It's a famously reclusive little town, about fourteen hundred people. And it has a fun real-estate story. In 1927 an old dairy farm on the mesa was divided into more than five thousand tiny lots, and a San Francisco newspaper sold a lot of them for 69 dollars and fifty cents each, as a promotion for subscriptions. Buy the paper, get some land! Some of those streets have since fallen into the sea. This is Buh-lee-nus Lagoon, a tidal estuary on the official list of wetlands of international importance. And yes, the San Andreas Fault runs right down the middle of it. Buh-lee-nus, over there, is on the Pacific Plate, sliding north from Stinson Beach at about an inch a year.

Stinson Beach! A long, sandy beach that San Franciscans have been escaping to for about 150 years. It started as Willow Camp, a tent settlement among the willows after the first coast road was built in 1870. After the 1906 earthquake, refugees from San Francisco came out and opened some of the first businesses, and in 1916 it was renamed after the biggest landowners, Rose and Nathan Stinson. Now: the Dipsea. Since 1905, runners have raced from Mill Valley, over the shoulder of Mount Tam, down to Stinson Beach. It's seven and a half miles with about 2,200 feet of climbing, and it's the oldest trail race in America. Runners can take shortcuts with names like Suicide and the Swoop. And older and younger runners get a head start of up to 25 minutes. Quiz: because of that handicap system, how young do you think the youngest winner was? [[pause 5]] Eight years old! And winners have been as old as seventy-two. Jack Kirk, the Dipsea Demon, ran 67 Dipseas in a row, and started his last one at 96. One word of warning: the water off here is in the Red Triangle, an area with unusually many great white shark attacks.

The big mountain above us is Mount Tam-ul-pie-iss, Mount Tam to the locals, 2,571 feet at the East Peak. Quiz: you might hear that Tam-ul-pie-iss means Sleeping Maiden, after a Mee-wok legend about the mountain's profile looking like a sleeping girl. True or false? [[pause 4]] False! That legend was made up in Victorian times, by a playwright for a play at the mountain's outdoor theatre. The name actually comes from the Coast Mee-wok tah-mal pah-heess, meaning west hill. From 1896 to 1930 a railroad wound up from Mill Valley to the summit, with so many bends it was nicknamed the Crookedest Railroad in the World. And in the 1970s, this mountain gave the world something new: the mountain bike. Riders bolted fat tires and better brakes onto old 1930s and 40s Schwinn bikes and bombed down the fire roads. Quiz: they held downhill races near Fairfax called the Repack races. Why Repack? [[pause 5]] Because the coaster brakes got so hot on the way down that the grease burned, and riders had to repack their wheel bearings after every race! Gary Fisher, Charlie Kelly and Joe Breeze were among the pioneers riding here.

Welcome to Muir Woods, one of the last old-growth redwood forests in the Bay Area. It's a narrow canyon on the slope of Mount Tam, wrapped in summer fog, which these trees drink up during the dry season. Here's how it survived. Mount Tam's redwoods were logged heavily to build San Francisco, and again to rebuild it after 1906. But the trees in this canyon, then called Redwood Canyon, were too hard to reach. In 1905, William Kent and his wife Elizabeth bought 611 acres of it for 45,000 dollars, with money borrowed from a banker friend, to save it. Then a water company tried to take part of it to build a dam and a reservoir. So Kent used a brand-new law, the Antiquities Act, and offered to donate the land to the nation. President Theodore Roosevelt accepted, and in January 1908 it became a national monument. Quiz: the name first suggested was the Kent Monument. What did Kent want instead? [[pause 4]] He insisted it be named after John Muir, the great naturalist! And the twist: Kent and Muir later fell out over damming the Hetch Hetchy valley, which Kent supported. Kent went on to Congress and sponsored the law creating the National Park Service in 1916. He was also, honestly, a loud supporter of anti-Asian immigration laws, so he's a complicated hero. The tallest tree here is 258 feet, most are 500 to 800 years old, and the oldest is at least 1,200. Quiz: how big is the seed a redwood grows from? [[pause 4]] About the size of a tomato seed! Tiny seed, giant tree.

One more Muir Woods story. In April 1945, delegates from 50 countries gathered in San Francisco to write the Charter of the United Nations. President Franklin Roosevelt was supposed to open the conference, but he died on the 12th of April, just before it started. So on the 19th of May, the delegates came out here to Cathedral Grove and held a ceremony in his memory, among the redwoods, and placed a plaque in his honor. It's still there. And a practical note: Muir Woods gets up to six thousand visitors a day at busy times, and parking is so limited that since 2018 you need a reservation to park or take the shuttle.

Let's talk about the coast redwood, Sequoia sempervirens. Quiz: how tall do you think the tallest living redwood is? [[pause 5]] About 381 feet! That's the tallest living tree on Earth, way up in Humboldt County. They can live about 2,000 years, and the trunks can be 29 feet across. Redwoods have been around a very long time. Their relatives' fossils go back to the age of the dinosaurs. They only grow in a narrow strip along the coast, from Big Sur up to the corner of Oregon, because they need that fog. In the dry summers, they drink moisture straight out of the fog. Before the Gold Rush, they covered about two million acres. Then the logging started, to build San Francisco and the towns all around it, including the Russian River towns we left this morning. Today only about 5 percent of the old-growth forest is left. The tallest and oldest trees survived in deep, steep canyons, partly because loggers simply couldn't get to them. That's exactly how Muir Woods made it.

Welcome to Petaluma! Quiz: Petaluma's old nickname was the Egg Capital of the World. And it had another nickname, a pun on the name. Can you guess it? [[pause 5]] Chickaluma! This town was all about chickens. It had the only known poultry drugstore, a pharmacy for chickens. And in 1879, Lyman Byce invented the coal-lamp egg incubator here. They still celebrate with a Butter and Eggs Day parade. The land was part of Rancho Peh-tuh-loo-muh, given in 1834 to our old friend General Vuh-lay-oh from Sonoma. In 1836 he built a huge adobe ranch house just east of town, the largest privately owned adobe ever built in California. It's a state historic park now. And here's a lucky break. In the 1906 earthquake, Petaluma was hardly damaged, thanks to stable bedrock underneath. So it became the base for rescue and relief across the county. That's also why downtown still has old iron-front buildings and Victorian houses. During the Depression nobody had the money to knock them down, and later people moving out from San Francisco restored them.

We're coming through San Rafael, the county seat of Marin. So who was Marin? The Coast Mee-wok have lived in Marin for about 6,500 years, and more than 600 of their village sites have been found. According to General Vuh-lay-oh, who chaired the committee that named California's counties in 1850, this county was named after Marin, a great Coast Mee-wok chief. His birth name was Weak-moo-say. He was baptized Marino at about the age of twenty, in 1801, and lived at Mission Dolores in San Francisco for years, often serving as godfather at baptisms. Vuh-lay-oh believed he'd fought fierce battles against the Spanish. Quiz: there's a rival theory for the county's name, involving the bay. What do you think? [[pause 5]] In 1775 the Spanish named the bay here Bah-ee-ah day Nwes-tra Sen-yora del Ro-sar-io la Mar-in-era, and Marin might just be short for that! Personally I'm going with the chief. And a movie fact: before moving to the Preh-sid-ee-oh in San Francisco, George Lucas's company Lucasfilm had its headquarters here in San Rafael.

This junction, where Highway 1 meets 101, is at the edge of Mill Valley, the town tucked into the redwood canyons on the side of Mount Tam. People have lived here a very long time. Fourteen Coast Mee-wok village sites have been found in the Mill Valley area, with huge shell mounds along Richardson Bay. One mound, excavated in 1907, was twenty feet high. And a plaque in a Mill Valley sidewalk marks the spot believed to be the birthplace of Chief Marin, in 1781. Quiz: right around this intersection, in 1916, a roadhouse was built that became famous during Prohibition. It was called the Blind Pig. Why do you think it was built here, outside the town? [[pause 5]] Because it was outside the dry laws, which were enforced more strictly inside the city itself. The roadhouses around here were known as gin joints, and worse. Mill Valley's also where the Dipsea Race starts, and where the Crookedest Railroad began its climb up Mount Tam.

Down to the left is Saw-suh-lee-toe, on Richardson Bay. The name is Spanish for small willow grove, and it's been spelled about a dozen different ways over the years. Before the bridge, Saw-suh-lee-toe was the end of the line: trains from up north, including that North Pacific Coast Railroad from the Russian River, met the ferries here. The car ferry to San Francisco took about twenty minutes and cost a dollar per car. In World War Two it became a shipbuilding center, and afterwards it turned arty and wealthy, famous for its houseboats. Quiz: when Saw-suh-lee-toe was laid out, planners assumed the town would one day expand by filling in the bay, like San Francisco did. So what's strange about some of Saw-suh-lee-toe's streets? [[pause 5]] They're underwater! Streets with names like Pescadero, Eureka and Teutonia were mapped out but are still under Richardson Bay. More than a fifth of the city is water.

Those wild green hills on your right, at the very tip of Marin, are the Marin Headlands. They look untouched, but they came close to being a city. Quiz: in the 1960s, the government sold more than 2,000 acres here to a developer who planned a whole new city called Mar-in-chello. How many people do you think it was meant for? [[pause 5]] 30,000! In 50 apartment towers, with houses, a shopping center and a hotel. In 1970 the developer lost a lawsuit, and the land was sold to the Golden Gate National Recreation Area instead. Phew. The headlands are dotted with old forts and gun batteries from the 1890s through World War Two, all built to keep enemy ships out of the bay, plus a Nike missile site from the Cold War. And Hawk Hill, 920 feet up, is the best place in the Pacific states to watch birds of prey. Every fall, tens of thousands of hawks, falcons, eagles and vultures funnel down the peninsula here, because they hate flying over water.

Here it is, everybody! The Golden Gate Bridge! Cameras up, passengers! It opened in 1937, and at that point it was the longest and tallest suspension bridge in the world. The towers are 746 feet tall, and the main span is 4,200 feet. Lots of experts said it couldn't be built, because of the wind, the fog, and the swirling tides. Quiz: the colour is called International Orange, chosen by the architect Irving Morrow. But the U.S. Navy had a different suggestion, to make it more visible to ships. What do you think the Navy wanted? [[pause 5]] Black and yellow stripes! Like a giant bumblebee. Thank goodness for Morrow. The chief engineer, Joseph Strauss, insisted on movable safety nets under the workers. Nineteen men were saved by those nets, and they formed a club, called the Half Way to Hell Club. Sadly eleven men did die, ten of them in a single accident in February 1937. And the numbers are wild. The two main cables contain about 80,000 miles of steel wire, enough to go around the Earth three times. Each tower has about 600,000 rivets. And 38 painters work on it all year round.

A few more bridge stories. During the Depression, the bridge district couldn't sell its bonds to pay for construction. Then in 1932, Amadeo Jah-nee-nee, the founder of Bank of America, bought the whole lot himself, to help the local economy. The day before cars were allowed on it, in May 1937, 200,000 people walked across. Some on roller skates! And for the fiftieth birthday in 1987, they closed it to cars again. Up to a million people showed up, around 300,000 crammed onto the bridge at once, and the curve in the middle of the deck actually flattened out under their weight. Engineers say it was designed to flex like that, but they haven't tried it again since. And the name of the strait came first. In 1846, John Free-mont named it Kry-sop-ih-lee, Golden Gate, after the Golden Horn harbor of Byzantium, as a golden gate to trade with Asia. The first Europeans known to sail through it were Juan de Ah-yah-luh's crew, in 1775.

Off the end of the bridge we're driving through the Preh-sid-ee-oh, a big wooded park that was a military base for 219 years. The Spanish founded it on the 17th of September, 1776. That's the same year as the American Declaration of Independence, on the other side of the continent. Then it passed to Mexico, then in 1848 to the U.S. Army, and in 1994 the Army handed it to the National Park Service. Congress told the Preh-sid-ee-oh to pay for itself, and it did, eight years early. Quiz: one of the Preh-sid-ee-oh's tenants makes some of the most famous movies in the world. George Lucas built his company's headquarters here, on the site of an old army hospital. Which company? [[pause 4]] Lucasfilm! Star Wars, from the Preh-sid-ee-oh. And the road we're on is the Preh-sid-ee-oh Parkway. The old Doyle Drive viaduct here was judged unsafe in an earthquake, so it was replaced with tunnels through the bluffs, for 1.1 billion dollars, finished in 2015. On top of the tunnels they built a 14-acre park called Preh-sid-ee-oh Tunnel Tops. So right now, people may be having a picnic on the roof of your road.

Nineteenth Avenue cuts right through Golden Gate Park. It's 1,017 acres, and gets about 24 million visitors a year. Quiz: before the park was built in the 1870s, what do you think covered three-quarters of this land? [[pause 4]] Sand dunes! This whole western side of the city was called the Outside Lands. Engineer William Hammond Hall and gardener John McLaren spent years planting grasses and trees to hold the sand in place. Hall later became California's first state engineer, and designed flood control for the Sacramento Valley, where this whole trip began. At the ocean end there are two Dutch-style windmills from 1903, which used to pump water around the park. Inside there's the de Young Museum, the California Academy of Sciences and the Japanese Tea Garden. And the Outside Lands music festival borrows that old name.

Welcome to San Francisco! Quick question: was this city always called San Francisco? [[pause 4]] Nope! It was a little trading settlement called Yerba Buena, Spanish for good herb. In January 1847, the American mayor renamed it San Francisco, after the mission founded here in 1776. And here's a callback for you: one reason was that General Vuh-lay-oh was planning a town called Francisca, after his wife. San Francisco grabbed the name first, so Vuh-lay-oh's town became Benicia instead, after his wife's middle name. In 1847 the town had about 459 people. Then gold was found, and it went from about 1,000 people in 1848 to 25,000 by December 1849. Ships arrived, and their crews deserted to go dig for gold, leaving a forest of empty masts in the harbor. Quiz: what happened to those roughly 500 abandoned ships? [[pause 5]] Some became warehouses, saloons and hotels. Many just rotted. And some were deliberately sunk, to claim the underwater land! Then the cove was filled in, so parts of downtown are literally built on top of Gold Rush ships. The cable cars started climbing Clay Street in 1873. The Beats took over North Beach in the 1950s, hippies flocked to Haight-Ashbury for the 1967 Summer of Love, and the city's been a magnet for misfits and dreamers ever since.

Okay, let's talk about the morning San Francisco fell down. At 5:12 a.m. on the 18th of April, 1906, the San Andreas Fault ruptured along about 280 miles of the coast. That's the same fault we followed past Toe-mah-less Bay and Buh-lee-nus this morning. A foreshock hit first, and then the main shaking lasted about 42 seconds. Magnitude about 7.9. Then came the fires, which burned for days. More than 3,000 people died, the deadliest earthquake in American history, and over 80 percent of the city was destroyed. At the time, San Francisco was the biggest city on the West Coast. Quiz: for years people thought the epicenter was up at Oh-lee-muh. Where do scientists now think it was? [[pause 5]] Offshore, near Mussel Rock by Daly City, the next town we drive through! And remember all the places we heard about today: refugees who started Stinson Beach businesses, Petaluma's relief efforts, the redwoods logged to rebuild the city. That earthquake shaped this whole region.

We're crossing into Daly City. After the 1906 earthquake, thousands of homeless San Franciscans headed south to the ranches here, including a big one belonging to John Daly, a dairyman who'd married his boss's daughter. The town grew from those refugees and took his name. Then, from the late 1940s, a developer called Henry Dole-ger built Westlake, one of the first big planned suburbs, with rows and rows of similar houses up the hillsides. Quiz: Westlake inspired a famous 1962 folk song by Malvina Reynolds, poking fun at rows of identical suburban houses. What's it called? [[pause 4]] Little Boxes! A sad note too: Filipino American families who wanted to buy here in the 1950s were barred from Westlake by racial covenants, so they bought homes east of Hoo-nee-peh-roe Serra Boulevard instead.

Here's the weirdest town on our whole trip: Colma. Most of its land is cemeteries. In 1900, San Francisco banned new burials inside the city, and in 1912 it evicted most of its existing cemeteries. So about 150,000 bodies were dug up and moved down here, at ten dollars per grave. Nearly everyone famous who died in San Francisco ended up here. Quiz: the dead here outnumber the living. By roughly how much? [[pause 5]] About a thousand to one! Somewhere around one and a half million people are buried here. It's been called the City of the Silent, and its unofficial motto is: It's great to be alive in Colma.

On the hills to the west is Sweeney Ridge. And something big happened up there. In 1769, the Spanish explorer Gaspar de Portolá was leading an expedition up the coast. He sent a scouting party, led by Sergeant José Ortega, north to find the Point Reyes headlands, which we drove past this morning. Ortega came back and reported he couldn't get there. Quiz: why not? [[pause 4]] Because the Golden Gate was in the way! He'd found the strait. And from Sweeney Ridge, on the 4th of November 1769, the expedition became the first Europeans known to see San Francisco Bay. Well, the scouts had actually spotted it a few days earlier. Amazing to think that all those sailors, Drake in 1579, Viz-kuh-ee-no in 1603, sailed right past one of the greatest harbors on Earth and never noticed it, hidden in the fog.

And here we are: San Francisco International Airport. Quiz, one last time: when the city opened its airport here in May 1927, what was the land being used for? [[pause 4]] It was a cow pasture! 150 acres, leased from the Mills family estate, as a temporary, experimental airport called Mills Field. In 1931 the city bought the land and named it San Francisco Airport, and international was added after World War Two. Pan Am moved its flying boats here in 1944. Funny detail: it's owned by San Francisco, but it's actually in San Mateo County. So, Julia, Adam, our heroic driver: that's a wrap! From Sacramento's Gold Rush to Napa's vineyards, the Russian River's redwoods, the Sonoma Coast, Point Reyes, Muir Woods and the Golden Gate. Volcanoes, earthquakes, Russians, Hitchcock and an egg capital. It's been an honour being your tour guide. Safe travels, come back soon, and remember: Goonies never say die!
